title: “The Emporium” is running at Classic Stage in NYC until June 7th only...
transcript: Why are my fellow theatre nerds not freaking out about this play's existence as much as I am? because I can't shut up about how fascinating it is on multiple levels not least of which is that the audience gets to vote at one point! Essentially, they discovered an unfinished play by one of the most important playwrights of the 20th century Thornton Wilder most famously the writer of Our Town. and this previously unproduced play was reconstructed and adapted from over 300 handwritten pages in Thornton Wilder's records it's called The Emporium, and it's about a mysterious department store and an orphan who spends his entire life trying to get a job there. but there are multiple meta layers surrounding it that I find exhilaratingly cool: first of all, obviously the context is part of the appeal here but it's fun that it happened with Thornton Wilder specifically of all playwrights who already leans into the meta theatrical so the adapter is actually able to incorporate some of the lore around this unfinished play into the production itself and it feels very much in the spirit of the writer. but it goes even further than that because the actual fact that the play was unfinished and unproduced echoes the themes in the play itself almost as if the things that Wilder was wrestling with that inspired him to write the play in the first place were the very same things that made it difficult for him to finish. and I just find that so endlessly fascinating especially because the adapter, Kirk Lynn, actually finds some really clever ways to heighten those parallels. we also get a lot of fun fourth wall breaks throughout the show sometimes the audience is asked to chime in with these call and response moments but the most memorable one comes about halfway through where they explain that there was a scene at the beginning of Act 2 in Wilder's original outline that he never actually wrote which would essentially reveal what the play was a metaphor for. so they explain that the adapter has written a version of this Act 2 prologue and we actually get to vote on whether we see it or not. the argument against it being that it might ruin the fun of interpreting the play for yourself especially because Wilder ultimately chose not to write it. but at my performance the audience, including myself l, voted overwhelmingly to yes, see the scene cause I definitely would have had FOMO otherwise plus I think the audience could use the help. which brings us to the question of like is this play actually good? honestly I'm not sure. I would say that it's a bit of a beautiful mess. it takes a relatively simple narrative through line and tells it in this bizarrely episodic way whiplashing us to different settings jumping forward in time at odd intervals and never quite locking into a coherent narrative flow. and yeah, it's partly a result of being a patchwork quilt of messy, unfinished fragments but you can also kinda tell that it comes partly from Thorton Wilder's own kooky storytelling sensibilities. by that same token though I also think you can feel some of that Thornton Wilder magic where he finds these odd, whimsical ways  of wrestling with the largest most overwhelming questions about what it means to be alive in this world. if Our Town is about mundanity Skin of our Teeth is about survival the Matchmaker is about joy and love, the Emporium, I guess, is about purpose and aspiration and he tackles it with the same aching human insight that made the rest of his work resonate so deeply
reasoning: Creator is fascinated by the meta context and recommends the experience enthusiastically, but openly hedges on whether the play itself is 'actually good,' calling it 'a beautiful mess.' The intellectual enthusiasm outweighs the narrative critique, landing in positive-with-caveats territory.
